questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x-2}+1 & <3 \\ 2{e}^{x-2} & <2 \\ {e}^{x-2} & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-2}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ x-2 & <0 \\ x & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}-\frac{3{e}^{2-3x}}{\sqrt{3}} & <-2\sqrt{3} \\ -\frac{3{e}^{2-3x}}{\sqrt{3}} & <-3\sqrt{3} \\ -3{e}^{2-3x} & <-3\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ -3{e}^{2-3x} & <-9 \\ {e}^{2-3x} & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2-3x}) & >\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 2-3x & >\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ -3x & >\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2 \\ 3x & <2-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x & <\frac{1}{3}(2-\operatorname{ln}⁡3).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(0.7)}^{x+9} & \ge 4 \\ {(0.7)}^{x+9} & \ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[(0.7)^{x+9}] & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ (x+9)\operatorname{ln}⁡0.7 & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡0.7$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+9 & \le \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡0.7} \\ x & \le \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡0.7}-9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}+1 & \ge 2 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6} & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}] & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ (x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6) & \le \frac{0}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x+6 & \le 0 \\ x & \le -6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(0.72)^{3x-7}+2 & \le -4 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0.72)^{3x-7} & \le -6 \\ (0.72)^{3x-7} & \le -12.\end{aligned}
$$

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than $0,$ we must have

$$
(0.72)^{3x-7}>0
$$

for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the inequality $(0.72)^{3x-7}\le -12$ has no solutions.

questions.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot {2}^{x} & <{3}^{2-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {2}^{x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2-x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡5+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2-x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & <(2-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & <2\operatorname{ln}⁡3-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & <2\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & <2\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ x & <\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$
